meta.title: The Objection the Letter Raised
meta.skill_frame: Argument and evidence: an objection the text raises and answers.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.32, 5.70 and 6.09 on the three parts (100, 101 and 111 words), 5.71 together. The load is a letter that states its own objection and answers it with a separate record, so the reader has to hold two problems apart.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for argument_evidence 4.1, band 4.1, sequence 5. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A swim club letter asking for new lane ropes that raises and answers the objection that cloudy water is the real problem.
source.avoided: No club name, pool name, or cost figure. No claim about who repairs the pumps.

session.difficulty_basis: The letter raises the objection itself and answers it with the pool log, so the reader must keep the rope problem and the cloud problem separate.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: The swim club asked the town to replace the lane ropes at the outdoor pool. The ropes are old, and paint comes off them into the water when swimmers brush against them. The club's letter makes its case in three parts. It describes the state of the ropes and the cost of new ones. Then it does something a weaker letter would leave out, which is to raise an objection against its own request. The letter spends a full page on that objection before it answers it. The club could have left the page out and sent a shorter case.
passage.part_2: The objection is that new ropes will not fix the pool, because the water is cloudy in August. The letter answers it with a record from the pool's own log. The pool was cloudy on nine days last August, and on every one of those days a pump had failed. The log was kept by the pool staff for their own repairs, and each cloudy day is tied to a repair. Nine cloudy days out of thirty-one is a lot of cloudy water for one month. The ropes are not named as the cause of the cloud on any page.
passage.part_3: That answer matters, because it keeps the objection from blocking the request. The club does not claim the ropes will clear the water. It shows that the water problem has a different cause, and the log names that cause. A reader can check the nine days against the log. An objection a letter answers well does more for the case than an objection the letter ignores. The club raised the question a reader would raise and closed it with a record, and the two problems stay apart. The town can price the ropes without worrying about the water. The log answers the question the club raised, and it answers with dates.

items.prompt: The letter does not claim the ropes will clear the water. Why does that help its case?

items.prompt: What would the letter have lost if it had left the objection out?
